posts.caption:
Selling into the EU under €150 just changed price.

Since 1 July 2026 the low value customs duty exemption is gone. Every consignment crossing the border now carries duty, at a flat €3 per tariff line, and that transitional rate runs until 1 July 2028.

Per tariff line is the part worth reading twice. The Council's own example is a parcel holding one silk blouse and two wool blouses. Different sub-headings, so two dutiable items, so €6. Ten of the same shirt in one parcel is still €3.

Two more dates belong in the calendar. New product identifiers become mandatory on 1 November 2026, and the EU handling fee is due to be set in autumn 2026, with member states free to add national charges on top.

The operational shift is quieter than the headline. A per tariff line duty rewards consolidation, so holding stock inside the EU turns a thousand dutiable parcels into one import. For a brand shipping into Germany from the US, that maths has moved.

Five things we would check now: tariff codes and origin, DDP or DAP, your EORI number, how your carrier declares low value parcels, and whether EU warehousing now pays for itself.

The German checkout stack, and why it decides your launch.

Five payment habits that decide whether a German launch converts.

Kauf auf Rechnung. Goods first, payment later, within 14 to 30 days. It is a trust convention, and offering it signals that you understand the market.

PayPal. Often the default here. Surfacing it early wins every customer who arrived with no intention of typing a card number.

SEPA direct debit. Anything recurring runs on it. Subscriptions and instalments in Germany are built this way.

Klarna. Buy now pay later is already normal online here, and Klarna is now expanding in store with retail partners.

Wero. The European Payments Initiative wallet is being integrated by German retailers, including Lidl's online store. Worth supporting before your competitors do.

Localisation means paying the way your customer already pays.

posts.caption:
They say you can guess someone's job from the laptop.

Left, a MacBook and a launch plan. Right, a laptop covered in stickers, with the BGB on the windowsill behind it.

That is Felicitas, Esq., Legal & Compliance at Axelwin, and she is qualified in Germany and in New York. One person, both legal systems. That is rarer than it sounds, and it is the reason a US brand can plan a German launch with the legal work running alongside it.

GDPR, incorporation, contracts, due diligence. Handled in both jurisdictions by the same person.

The route runs both ways. A German brand opening in the US gets the same pairing in reverse.

Cleared for launch.

#germanmarketentry #dtcbrands #ecommercelaw #hamburg

Five points where a German launch gets stopped.

Trademark. A US registration protects nothing in Germany or the EU, so clearance and filing belong at the start of the project, well before the first cease and desist letter.

Impressum. Germany requires a full legal notice page, with named representatives and registration details publicly listed. Publishing it keeps you clear of the Abmahnung.

Consent. Cookie banners that assume agreement, or arrive pre-ticked, fall short of the German standard, and enforcement here is private as well as regulatory.

Packaging. VerpackG has required packaging registration for years, and from 12 August 2026 PPWR adds an authorised representative in every member state you sell into.

Returns. Statutory withdrawal rights override a US drafted returns policy. The clause written in New York is unenforceable in Hamburg.

Cleared for launch is the whole point of in-house German and New York lawyers on every Axelwin engagement. The five points above are handled before your launch date.

German ecommerce is growing again, and Germany is still the key to Europe.

Revenue grew 4.3 percent in the first half of 2026, and 5.1 percent in the second quarter alone. The largest ecommerce market in the EU is expanding.

Where a brand starts depends on product market fit, and that answer is different every time. What holds is what Germany does to a business. The payment habits, the consumer law, the returns culture and a buyer who researches harder than almost anywhere else make it the most demanding market in Europe. Make it work here and Austria, Switzerland and the Netherlands run off the same operational base.
